issues.legal_issue: A writ court cannot compel a municipality to provide a stall or alternative site where doing so would conflict with the prohibition on unpermitted structures on public streets and the municipality’s power to remove encroachments.
material_facts: The respondent occupied a pavement site under a tehbazari licence, but the trial court had disallowed her claim to an injunction against removal of any stall or structure placed there.
The High Court relied on an earlier consent order to direct the municipality to construct a stall for the respondent or provide a sanctioned plan for her to build one.
The earlier order did not decide whether the municipality had a statutory duty to provide an alternative site before removing an encroachment.
The pavement site was a public place, and the governing law prohibited structures there without the Commissioner’s permission and empowered the Commissioner to remove encroachments.
issues.conclusion: The High Court’s direction to provide a stall or plan was contrary to law and could not stand; the municipality had no statutory obligation to provide an alternative site as a condition precedent to removing an encroachment.
issues.legal_principle: Section 320(1) of the Delhi Municipal Corporation Act, 1957 bars erection or setting up of a structure in or upon a street without the Commissioner’s permission. Section 322(a) empowers the Commissioner to remove an encroaching structure from a public place. A court cannot grant mandamus that would require conduct contrary to those provisions. The Court distinguished the consent order in Jamna Das, which expressed no opinion on any statutory duty to provide an alternative site.

predicates.writ_proceeding_seeks_forced_stall_provi: A person brings a writ proceeding seeking an order that a public authority provide a stall or authorize its construction on a public way.
predicates.unpermitted_structure_on_public_way: A structure is placed on a public way without the permission required for placing it there.
predicates.requested_relief_would_conflict_with_rem: The requested order would prevent or condition the public authority’s exercise of its power to remove an encroachment.

issues.definition: When a writ proceeding seeks forced stall provision and the structure is unpermitted or the requested relief conflicts with removal authority, the court cannot compel stall provision or make an alternative site a precondition to removal.

issues.legal_issue: A consent order expressly reserved from precedential use, or made without argument or consideration of the point later raised, does not bind a later court as precedent on that point.
material_facts: The earlier court directed rehabilitation by constructing stalls after counsel for the parties requested a direction and undertook to comply.
The earlier court expressly stated that its direction was not to be treated as a precedent.
The earlier order did not address the statutory provisions governing removal of public-way encroachments or decide whether an alternative site had to be provided.
The High Court relied on that order in directing relief for another pavement occupant.
issues.conclusion: The earlier consent order was not a binding precedent on whether an alternative site had to be provided, and the High Court was not bound to follow it.
issues.legal_principle: Only the ratio decidendi of a case is binding; statements outside the ratio are obiter dicta. A consent order does not adjudicate the parties’ rights or lay down a principle. A decision made without argument or consideration of a point is not authority on that point, and a decision given in ignorance of a relevant statute may be per incuriam. The Court referred to Salmond on Jurisprudence, Gerard v. Worth of Paris Ltd. and Lancaster Motor Co. (London) Ltd. v. Bremith Ltd.

predicates.later_court_is_asked_to_follow_prior_ord: A court in a later proceeding is asked to treat an earlier judicial order as controlling authority.
predicates.prior_order_was_by_consent_and_disclaime: The earlier order was made by consent and expressly stated not to be treated as a precedent.
predicates.relevant_legal_point_was_not_argued_or_c: The earlier court did not hear argument on or consider the legal point for which the order is later cited.

issues.definition: When a later court is asked to follow an order made by consent with an express reservation, or one that did not consider the relevant point, that order is not binding precedent on that point.

issues.legal_issue: A party cannot raise a livelihood-based constitutional claim for the first time on appeal when it was not pleaded or advanced below and the parties’ rights are already governed by a final decree.
material_facts: The respondent did not plead in her writ petition or argue before the High Court that removal of the encroachment threatened her right to life or that life included a right to livelihood.
An unappealed civil decree had already settled the parties’ rights concerning the respondent’s occupation and the termination of her licence.
On appeal, counsel sought to rely on Olga Tellis and Bombay Hawkers’ Union to raise the livelihood argument.

The Court noted that Olga Tellis recognized livelihood as part of life but upheld statutory removal powers, and Bombay Hawkers’ Union treated restrictions on hawking as reasonable in the public interest.
issues.conclusion: The Court would not permit the livelihood-based constitutional question to be raised in the appeal.
issues.legal_principle: The Court declined to consider the Article 21 argument because it had not been raised in the writ petition or before the High Court and because the parties’ rights had been crystallized by a final decree. Olga Tellis v. Bombay Municipal Corporation and Bombay Hawkers’ Union v. Bombay Municipal Corporation were distinguished as not supporting the new argument in these circumstances.

predicates.appeal_from_writ_decision: A party appeals from a court’s decision in a writ proceeding.
predicates.livelihood_claim_not_raised_below: The party did not plead or argue the livelihood-based constitutional claim in the courts below.
predicates.parties_rights_fixed_by_final_decree: An unappealed final decree has already settled the rights between the parties relevant to the dispute.

issues.definition: In an appeal from a writ decision, a livelihood claim not raised below cannot be considered when a final decree has already fixed the parties’ relevant rights.

issues.legal_issue: An unappealed decree governing a licensee’s occupation remains binding between the parties and must be followed even when an appellate court sets aside later writ relief.
material_facts: The trial court permanently restrained the municipality from removing the respondent from the licensed site without terminating her permission according to the applicable procedure.
The trial court disallowed an injunction against demolition or removal of any stall or other structure.
The municipality did not appeal the decree, which had become final between the parties.
The Supreme Court allowed the municipality’s appeal against the High Court’s later direction but expressly directed the municipality to act in conformity with the final trial court decree.
issues.conclusion: The municipality must act in conformity with the unappealed decree governing the respondent’s occupation and the termination of her licence.
issues.legal_principle: A decree that has not been appealed and has become final between the parties crystallizes their rights; those rights must be worked out in accordance with the decree. The Court therefore set aside the High Court’s additional relief while preserving the binding effect of the trial court decree.

predicates.appeal_involves_rights_governed_by_final: An appeal concerns rights between parties that have been addressed by a trial court decree.
predicates.decree_was_not_appealed: The party against whom the decree operates did not appeal it, and it became final between the parties.

issues.definition: When an appeal concerns rights governed by an unappealed final decree, the public authority must comply with that decree between the parties.
